For inbound traffic flow from your on-premises network to AWS, you must use preferred routing options to set the preference to a particular path.\\\\n\\\\nTo manage asymmetric routing with Direct Connect, use prefix length and Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) attributes to determine path selection for different types of virtual interfaces.\\\\n\\\\n**Note:** For public virtual interfaces, AWS uses AS\\\\\\\\_PATH and the [longest prefix match](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/influencing-traffic-over-hybrid-networks-using-longest-prefix-match/) to determine the routing path\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-manage-asymmetric-routing\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Direct Connect routing policies and BGP communities\",\"context\":\"## Private virtual interface and transit virtual interface routing policies\\\\n\\\\nIf you\\'re using AWS Direct Connect to access your private AWS resources,\\\\nyou must specify the IPv4 or IPv6 prefixes to advertise over BGP. These prefixes can be\\\\npublic or private.\\\\n\\\\nThe following outbound routing rules apply based on the prefixes advertised:\\\\n\\\\n* AWS evaluates the longest prefix length first. AWS recommends advertising\\\\n more specific routes using multiple Direct Connect virtual interfaces if the\\\\n desired routing paths are meant for active/passive connections. See Influencing Traffic over Hybrid Networks using Longest Prefix\\\\n Match for more information.\\\\n* Local preference is the BGP attribute recommended to use when desired routing\\\\n paths are meant for active/passive connections and the prefix lengths advertised\\\\n are the same. This value is set per Region to prefer Direct\\\\n Connect locations that have the same associated AWS Region using the\\\\n `7224:7200`\u2014Medium local preference community value. Where\\\\n the local Region is not associated with the Direct Connect\\\\n location, it is set to a lower value. This applies only if no local preference\\\\n community tags are assigned. For more information about associated Regions, see\\\\n Associated Region.\\\\n* AS_PATH length can be used to determine the routing path when the prefix\\\\n length and local preference are the same.\\\\n* Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED) can be used to determine the routing path when\\\\n prefix length, local preference, and AS_PATH are the same. AWS does not\\\\n recommend using MED values given their lower priority in evaluation.\\\\n* AWS uses equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) routing across multiple transit or\\\\n private virtual interfaces when prefixes have the same AS_PATH length and BGP\\\\n attributes. The ASNs in the AS_PATH of the prefixes do not need to match\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Influencing Traffic over Hybrid Networks using Longest Prefix Match | Networking & Content Delivery\",\"context\":\"### Data Center to AWS\\\\n\\\\nWe can also use LPM to influence traffic in the reverse direction. Let\u2019s suppose we want traffic originating from PHX to reach a destination resource in US-West-1 (10.0.0.0/16) with the local Direct Connect as the primary path and the MPLS as the secondary. The destination resource is in a VPC with IP address of 10.0.0.101.\\\\n\\\\nIn this case, we want the routes advertised from the PHX Direct Connect Gateway to be more specific than the routes advertised across MPLS. To do this, we go to the AWS console and enter 10.0.0.0/17 and 10.0.128.17 as the IP prefixes to be advertised from AWS to PHX via Allowed prefixes under Direct Connect gateway association as shown in Figure 12:\\\\n\\\\nFigure 12: Use LPM to prefer local Direct Connect as Primary to US-West-1\\\\n\\\\nThe resulting route table in PHX customer router would then look as shown in Table 4:\\\\n\\\\n| | |\\\\n| --- | --- |\\\\n| **Destination (Prefix)** | **Target (Next Hop)** |\\\\n| 10.0.0.0/17 | Direct Connect |\\\\n| 10.0.128.0/17 | Direct Connect |\\\\n| 10.0.0.0/16 | MPLS |\\\\n\\\\nTable 4: PHX Route Table\\\\n\\\\nBecause the routes using the /17 prefix are more specific, the PHX router will use its local Direct Connect as its primary path to reach the 10.0.0.101 destination in US-West-1. If the local Direct Connect in PHX is disrupted, the PHX router will failover to the next matching path (10.0.0.0/16) over MPLS, and then through US-East-1 to reach its destination in US-West-1 as shown on Figure 13:\\\\n\\\\nFigure 13: Failover to MPLS to reach US-West-1\\\\n\\\\nThe return traffic from US-West-1 would follow the same path in the reverse direction as shown in Figure 14:\\\\n\\\\nFigure 14: Return Traffic from US-West-1 to PHX\\\\n\\\\nOne thing to remember is that BGP is used to advertise routes between the AWS and the data centers but not between the Transit Gateway peers. Therefore, static routes need to be manually entered into each Transit Gateway in order to route traffic between Transit Gateway peers\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/influencing-traffic-over-hybrid-networks-using-longest-prefix-match/\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. {"id": "722f68fa-f604-4a5a-a106-11ace4dac158", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "I don't see a document specifically titled "DX Path Selection Flow Chart" in AWS's official documentation. There's no single named flow chart doc for this — AWS instead spreads the path-selection logic across a few sources:

- **[Direct Connect routing policies and BGP communities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html)** — the authoritative reference. It lays out the evaluation order AWS uses for outbound path selection: longest prefix match first, then local preference (BGP community `7224:7200` for same-Region DX locations), then AS_PATH length, then MED, with ECMP applied when everything ties.
- **[Influencing Traffic over Hybrid Networks using Longest Prefix Match](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/influencing-traffic-over-hybrid-networks-using-longest-prefix-match/)** — a Networking & Content Delivery blog post that does include actual flow diagrams/figures (e.g., Figure 12–14) showing primary vs. failover path selection, which is probably the closest thing to a visual "flow chart" AWS publishes.
- **[How do I manage asymmetric routing with Direct Connect?](https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-manage-asymmetric-routing)** — a re:Post knowledge center article on controlling inbound vs. outbound path symmetry.

If you need something citable for a design doc, the routing-and-bgp.html UserGuide page is the right primary citation since it's the canonical reference AWS maintains; the blog post is good supplementary citation if you want the visual diagrams.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
